name: Neon
license: Proprietary service; the storage engine and Postgres changes are Apache 2.0 on GitHub
summary: Serverless Postgres that keeps data in a shared storage layer, so compute can scale to zero and a branch of the database is a pointer, not a copy.
intro: Neon splits Postgres in two. A compute node runs ordinary Postgres (14 to 18) with RAM and a local NVMe cache, but owns no durable state. Instead of writing WAL to its own disk, it streams WAL to several safekeepers, and a commit succeeds once a quorum of them acknowledges it through a Paxos-based protocol. Pageservers turn that WAL into data pages and upload them to object storage as immutable layer files. When compute misses a page in its caches, it asks a pageserver for the page as of a log position (`GetPage@LSN`), and the pageserver rebuilds it from the nearest image plus later WAL. Because old versions are never overwritten, a branch is a copy-on-write view of a past position, and restoring to any moment in the history window is the same operation. Storage is spread across availability zones; there are no standby computes, and a failed compute is restarted, typically within seconds to minutes.

Neon has belonged to Databricks since 2025, and the same engine now runs both as Neon, for developers and agent platforms, and as Databricks Lakebase. It runs in 8 AWS regions and is billed by usage, with no monthly minimum. As checked on 2026-10-06: the Free plan gives 100 projects, each with 100 CU-hours a month (a CU is about 4 GB of RAM) and 1 GB of storage. Launch costs $0.106 per CU-hour and Scale $0.222, with storage at $0.35 per GB-month and history at $0.20 per GB-month of retained WAL. Compute scales to zero after 5 minutes idle and wakes in a few hundred milliseconds.
strengths: Branches are instant copy-on-write views, so every pull request, test run or agent can get a full copy of production that costs nothing until it diverges
Scale to zero and autoscaling, billed per CU-hour: idle databases cost only storage, and the Free plan covers 100 small projects
Point-in-time restore and branching from the past without backups, within a history window of up to 7 days (Launch) or 30 days (Scale)
Standard Postgres with extensions such as pgvector, PostGIS and TimescaleDB, and PgBouncer pooling up to 10,000 connections
Commits are durable once a quorum of safekeepers in different zones has the WAL, with a secondary pageserver ready if one fails
limits: No standby compute on Neon: if compute fails it is restarted, so applications must handle disconnects of seconds to minutes; high availability is listed as coming soon, while Lakebase on Databricks has it
Waking from zero adds a few hundred milliseconds; computes above 16 CU never scale to zero, and connected logical replication subscribers keep compute running

Storage bills have several parts: retained WAL in the history window, child branches that become as expensive as a root once they fall out of that window, and $1.50 a month per branch beyond the 10 or 25 included
AWS only now: Azure regions stopped taking new projects on 7 April 2026 and stopped getting features on 5 October 2026, and a project can’t change region
The public GitHub repo went from hundreds of commits a month to a handful after July 2025, with no tagged release since; its README covers running Neon on a workstation for small experiments

story: Postgres ties a database to one machine and its disk. Scaling means migrating to a bigger machine, failover means paying for whole extra servers, and a realistic copy for development means copying all the data. Amazon Aurora and Microsoft’s Socrates had shown that a database could replace its local disk with a shared storage service, but none of those designs were open source or native to Postgres.

Nikita Shamgunov, Heikki Linnakangas, a Postgres committer, and Stas Kelvich started Neon in 2021 to rebuild Postgres storage for the cloud without forking Postgres. Heikki integrated the storage with upstream Postgres, and Stas built the storage layer and WAL streaming. Their twist on Aurora was to make object storage the home of all history, which made branches and time travel cheap. Neon launched publicly in June 2022 behind a waitlist, released its code under Apache 2.0, and became generally available in April 2024 after scaling to more than 700,000 databases.

By 2025 more than 80% of new Neon databases were being created by AI agents rather than people. Databricks announced it would acquire Neon on 14 May 2025, and the engine became the base of Databricks Lakebase as well as Neon itself.

choices.why: Aurora used one storage service, Microsoft’s later SQL Server design two. Neon chose two: the consensus code is easier to verify on its own, and safekeepers only append while pageservers read, write and update, so each can run on hardware suited to it.

choices.choice: Stream WAL out and read pages back, without forking Postgres
choices.why: Postgres already writes every change as WAL records that name the pages they touch. Sending them over the network and fetching pages by RPC needed only small changes to Postgres, so users keep full compatibility.

choices.choice: Treat old page versions like current ones
choices.why: Read replicas and point-in-time recovery both need old pages. Keeping every version, with cold data moved to object storage, replaced backups and the WAL archive and made restoring or branching from the past a cheap lookup instead of hours of replay.
Tools such as Delphix built database copies on ZFS, but a filesystem the team didn’t control would be hard to integrate with the cloud and expensive, so they built storage that understands Postgres.

timeline.text: Shamgunov, Linnakangas and Kelvich start Neon; code on GitHub from March
Public launch behind a waitlist in June
Databricks announces the acquisition on 14 May; prices cut through the year
Azure regions deprecated in April; Neon runs on AWS only
